But the true measure of youth sports' success – the score that really matters – is how many lifelong athletes it creates.

articles.title: Dining with someone you love may help the body in surprising ways, new research suggests
articles.summary: A compelling study suggests that eating with a close partner could lead to lower blood sugar spikes, with glucose levels returning to normal more quickly. Fox News Digital spoke to experts.
articles.body: Eating with a close partner may influence the body in a surprising way, new research suggests. While researchers say the effect varies from person to person, a recent study suggests that eating with a loved one impacts how the body regulates blood sugar after a meal. Participants in the study were given meals containing the same amount and type of carbohydrates, and researchers measured their blood glucose after eating. THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW When participants ate together, researchers observed a smaller rise in glucose and a quicker return toward baseline compared with when they ate alone. The findings, however, do not mean that everyone will experience the same effect. Shir Atzil, Ph.D., the study's co-author and a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel, told Fox News Digital that researchers observed substantial individual differences. "While we observe the principle of social physiology at the population level, we have seen tremendous individual differences in how much individuals benefit or even actually lose from being together — so not everyone benefits the same amount," Atzil said. "Some people gain a huge benefit from being with their partners," she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Some people gain a small benefit — and some people actually regulate themselves better when they're alone." The research, published in the journal Science Advances in late September, was based on a concept known as social physiology, which examines how being near a close partner may affect physiological processes. Atzil described the theory as suggesting that "our most basic physiological processes, [our] bodily homeostasis, the process of just keeping the body up and running, is actually working more efficiently when we're in proximity with a close partner." More research is needed to understand why people respond differently, Atzil emphasized. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She said she plans to continue testing the social physiology theory. Social setting is also only one of many factors that can affect blood glucose. Erin Palinski-Wade, a New York-area registered dietitian specializing in diabetes, told Fox News Digital that the amount and type of carbohydrates consumed are particularly important. She noted that blood sugar can also be affected by factors including stress, sleep, physical activity and a person's surroundings. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Stress, whether you had [quality sleep] the night before, how active you were that day, even things like the temperature of the room, noise pollution — all of those things can impact blood sugar," Palinski-Wade said. Persistently elevated glucose can contribute to serious health problems over time. Regulating blood sugar after meals is important because persistently elevated glucose can contribute to serious health problems over time, including heart, kidney, eye and nerve damage, according to the National Institutes of Health. articles.title: One group of married Americans is having more sex — and happier marriages
articles.summary: Institute for Family Studies research finds regular churchgoers report more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than nonreligious spouses.
articles.body: Married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all, according to a new report from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS) in Charlottesville, Virginia. Researchers analyzed findings from multiple datasets, including the 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey of 3,125 married adults ages 18–54, the long-running nationally representative General Social Survey, and a separate survey of 1,219 alumni of FOCUS, a Catholic campus ministry. Regular churchgoers reported having more frequent sex than less religious or non-religious married adults, with regularly attending Catholics reporting some of the highest levels of sexual frequency. The association remained even after accounting for demographic differences. COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS Among married adults ages 20 to 54, 62% of regular churchgoers reported having sex at least once a week, compared with 48% of nonreligious spouses, according to the report. In addition to frequency, sexual satisfaction was also higher among church attendants. Catholics and Protestants who regularly attended religious services were more likely to rate their sex lives positively than those who attended less often or had no religious affiliation. Daily prayer was linked to greater sexual satisfaction among married Catholics and Protestants, though it was not associated with more frequent sex. Among churchgoers, 55% of Catholics and 45% of Protestants rated their sex lives as "excellent" or "very good," compared with 45% of nominal Catholics, 35% of nominal Protestants and 40% of religiously unaffiliated respondents. ‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT Those who viewed marriage as a permanent commitment were more likely to report both frequent and satisfying sex. That belief, along with shared values, was also strongly associated with overall marital quality. Study limitations Because the analysis was observational, it cannot determine whether religious practice directly causes better marital or sexual outcomes, the authors acknowledged. Additionally, the marital outcomes were self-reported, and other unmeasured differences between religious and non-religious respondents could have influenced the results. Differences in factors such as age and length of marriage could also make it challenging to strike comparisons with the broader population. The study was funded by FOCUS, the Fellowship of Catholic University Students. Marriage therapist reacts Jessica Steinman, a licensed marriage and family therapist and certified sex addiction therapist in Los Angeles, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential relationship between religious activity and the quality of a couple’s sex life. "When we think of people who are really involved in religion … we might think they're not having a lot of sex or that they're having very constricted views on their sex lives," she said. "And this article and research show that's changing." WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID People who actively participate in a shared spiritual or religious life may also feel more connected to one another as partners, according to Steinman, who is also the chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, Chicago and Austin. "If they're showing up and looking at things outside themselves — things that are spiritual, things that are religious, things are having them look inward, things that are having them look into larger morals and values within their marriages and partnerships — I think they're going to possibly have happier marriages and partnerships," the therapist said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES They may also be more vulnerable and open with one another, which could contribute to a more active sex life, she added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The rituals and shared practices associated with religious life likely play a role in strengthening that connection, the expert suggested. "Certain religious settings are really focused on rituals and traditions," Steinman said. "And if you're looking at partnership and marriage … engaging in sexual connection and sexual intimacy can really become a ritual itself." The research highlighted what has been described as an ongoing "sex recession," where people are not engaging in sexual intimacy as much as they once did. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Regardless of religious affiliation, Steinman encourages people to find ways to connect with their partners. "Get off the phones, get off of the internet, turn the TV off and start really connecting with your partner," she advised. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Steinman suggested that partners engage with one another and build connections that go deeper than simply asking, "How was your day?" That can include building emotional openness and discussing how partners want to connect sexually, she said.

articles.title: Accident near Hebbal flyover in Bengaluru turns into extortion ordeal, alleges engineer
articles.summary: Bengaluru engineer alleges extortion after Hebbal flyover accident; two men forced him to transfer Rs 6,000 via QR code. Police book case under Section 308.
articles.body: Bengaluru: A road accident near Hebbal flyover allegedly took an unexpected turn when a 25-year-old mechanical engineer was forced to transfer Rs 6,000 after two men reportedly threatened and manhandled him while he was nursing a fractured arm.According to the complaint filed by Aswin M Puthumana, an employee at a private firm in Bhadrappa Layout, he was riding his Royal Enfield Guerrilla bike from BEL football ground towards his PG accommodation in Veeranapalya around 11 pm on Sept 29 when an electric scooter, bearing registration number KA-01-AS-1374, collided with his bike near Hebbal Circle junction.Speaking to TOI, he said, soon after he met with the accident, he fell unconscious for a few seconds and later, two men took him in an autorickshaw, bearing registration number KA-03-AF-9820, claiming they were taking him to a nearby Baptist hospital.The two claimed to be the brothers of the person who had caused the accident. They demanded money towards repairs to their brother’s damaged scooter. He told them he did not have any money and that his own motorcycle had also been damaged in the accident.According to Aswin, the duo stopped a little ahead of the hospital on a service road and began arguing that he had come on the wrong side of the road and was responsible for the accident. Aswin said, “I was on the correct side; the electric scooter rider was on the wrong side.”Aswin alleged the men then picked a quarrel with him, claiming their younger brother had suffered injuries and demanding for money. When he refused, one of them threatened to hit him. Aswin, who had fractured his left arm after falling from his bike, said one of them pressed hard on the injured arm, causing him severe pain.A delivery boy, who witnessed the accident, had followed the auto. articles.title: Silent heart threat found in adults under 30 with no known cardiovascular disease
articles.summary: Silent artery plaque was detected in over half of healthy adults in the REACT study, yet traditional cardiovascular risk scores missed many of those cases.
articles.body: A buildup of artery-clogging plaque may begin much earlier than many people realize, new research has found. About 1 in 13 adults ages 18 to 29 already had silent atherosclerosis — the hardening of the arteries from plaque — despite having no known cardiovascular disease, while more than half of all healthy adults in the study showed signs of plaque somewhere in their arteries, according to a major new international study. Researchers from Denmark and Spain used advanced imaging to examine more than 16,800 adults ages 18 to 70 with no known cardiovascular disease. They found plaque in 57.1% of participants, with prevalence increasing steadily with age, from about 1 in 13 adults under 30 to roughly 9 in 10 adults ages 60 to 70, according to the research published in The New England Journal of Medicine in August. EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE Atherosclerosis occurs when fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up inside arteries, according to experts. The process often develops silently over many years before causing a heart attack or stroke. "For decades, we have estimated cardiovascular risk using factors such as age, blood pressure and cholesterol," Dr. Borja Ibáñez, a cardiologist and scientific director of Spain's National Center for Cardiovascular Research (CNIC), said in a statement. "This study shows that we can now go one step further and detect the disease directly before it causes a heart attack or stroke." COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY The new findings come from the first phase of the ongoing international REACT study, which is mapping how common silent artery plaque is across adulthood. In the next phase, researchers will test whether earlier detection can improve heart disease prevention. "Until now, preventive decisions have been based on an estimate of risk, but we did not know whether the disease was already present," Professor Henning Bundgaard, professor of cardiology at Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen, said. "REACT shows that atherosclerosis can be detected decades before clinical manifestations appear and provides the most comprehensive atlas of the evolution of the disease across adult life." MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS The study also revealed that men tended to develop plaque five to 10 years earlier than women, while women experienced their steepest increase between ages 40 and 60. Researchers also found that commonly used cardiovascular risk scores only identified a small proportion of people who already had silent atherosclerosis, suggesting some cases may go undetected using traditional risk assessments alone. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS While the researchers believe portable ultrasound could eventually help identify hidden plaque earlier, they said further clinical trials are needed. The findings should encourage people to take heart health seriously, but not to panic, experts note. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Finding plaque doesn't mean someone is about to have a heart attack, but finding it gives us an opportunity to address a patient's risk factors," Dr. Sirisha Vadali, a cardiologist at HonorHealth Women’s Heart Health in Arizona, told Fox News Digital. "We shouldn't wait for symptoms to start paying attention to heart health." "Feeling healthy doesn't necessarily mean your arteries are free of plaque," Vadali, who was not involved in the research, added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ She cautioned that the study alone does not establish that screening everyone will directly prevent heart attacks or strokes. Vadali stressed that the findings do not mean everyone under 30 should undergo artery screening, saying decisions about additional testing should be based on a person's individual risk factors. She recommended avoiding tobacco, staying physically active and eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, beans, whole grains, nuts and fish while limiting saturated fat and excess sodium to help protect heart health. articles.title: CM releases Didi’s 2021 med report, calls leg injury false
articles.summary: Suvendu Adhikari cites 2021 SSKM/Bangur reports to dispute Mamata Banerjee’s leg injury claim; TMC calls it privacy breach, CID probing.
articles.body: Kolkata: CM Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday made public a five-year-old medical report by Bangur Institute of Neurosciences to claim that Mamata Banerjee’s leg injury in the run-up to the 2021 Bengal assembly elections was “false”. The CID was probing the case, he added.Trinamool also released a five-year-old image of Banerjee’s bleeding left knee, saying it was illegal to make confidential medical reports public, and dubbed the CM’s statement “tasteless filth-mongering”.Banerjee had injured her left knee during election campaign in Nandigram’s Birulia on March 11, 2021.Showing medical records, Adhikari said: “During a speech in Nandigram on Friday, I said that in 2021, the whole of Nandigram was insulted by the then CM. Her leg was allegedly broken. I have the report from Bangur Institute of Neurosciences, dept of radiodiagnosis, dated 11.03.21, which says there was no evidence of fracture or dislocation.”The SSKM medical report read: “No evidence of fracture/dislocation.” A second report read: “No bony injury seen.”“I am not saying anything extra as of now. CID is probing the case; once the election model code of conduct is lifted, I will initiate a fresh probe into this false propaganda. Just as an investigation takes place when you file a complaint, action can also be taken against you if you make a false complaint. I will inform you about this after Oct 9,” Adhikari said.The Nandigram bypoll is scheduled for Oct 6, with the results set to be declared on Oct 9. In the 2021 assembly polls, Adhikari defeated Banerjee by 1,956 votes, a result that has been challenged in Calcutta High Court. The matter is sub judice.Trinamool spokesperson Kunal Ghosh cited National Medical Commission rules and the Supreme Court’s ruling on the right to privacy and said: “His vile politics ahead of the bypolls is reprehensible and condemnable. It is once again proven that Mamata-di is whom BJP considers the real opposition... Moreover, doctors and institutions never have the practice of disclosing anyone’s personal medical information outside, and govt should remember that too. How much further will they drag politics down?”Ghosh added, “Slandering and spreading misinformation about anyone’s personal injury is reprehensible. Mamata-di had a foot injury and the doctors concerned are witnesses to that. The CM should understand that even if something breaks (fractures), it can be set or healed. But a deep injury to soft tissue, muscle and bone is hard to heal completely. Even now, the swelling on Mamata-di’s foot is not normal.”Bengal BJP spokesperson Debjit Sarkar, posting Banerjee’s medical reports on his X handle, said: “Now, the truth lies bare and open. Mamata Banerjee’s entire act of being in a hospital with a bandage around her leg was nothing but exaggerated drama.”Adhikari, while campaigning for BJP’s Nandigram candidate Hasirani Rath on Friday evening — incidentally in Birulia as well — raked up the issue first. He said: “I do not like personal attacks. After becoming CM, I went to SSKM Hospital. I am chairman (of Rogi Kalyan Samiti) there. X-ray plates are usually handed over to the patient, not kept by the doctor; only the report remains. Didn’t she bring disgrace upon all of you that day? The car door had struck an iron beam, it swung back and lightly hit her leg. Yet she roamed around with a bandage, claiming her leg was broken. I still have those papers with me. She was the CM then. Her own doctors had written that there was no fracture. If needed, and if challenged, I will produce them. I am also the police minister now. I will show how she insulted all of Birulia and Nandigram.”Campaigning for Nandigram bypoll ends on Sunday evening. articles.summary: 66 people, including 45 women, fell ill in Ballia after eating madua flour roti and bati during pre-Jyutiya rituals; flour traced to one mill and shop.

articles.title: Caitlin Cark was part of the greatest tradition in sports on college football Saturday
articles.summary: The WNBA star felt right at home.
articles.body:
Caitlin Cark got to take in one of the greatest traditions in sports from Stead Family Children's Hospital on Saturday.

The WNBA star and former Iowa Hawkeyes great took part in Iowa's Hawkeye Wave during the Ohio State game. What made this unique was Clark was with the kids in the hospital looking down on the stadium. She was the guest picker earlier in the day for ESPN's College GameDay, but didn't want to leave without being part of the tradition.

Clark wasn't the one who added to Iowa's famed gesture. Ohio State coach Ryan Day sent a letter to each child at the Iowa Stead Family Children's Hospital ahead of Saturday's game.

When the stadium clock hit zero at the end of the first quarter, 70,000 football fans turned their attention from the field to UI Stead Family Children's Hospital. Everyone waves to the pediatric patients and their families watching the game. This genuine act of kindness is what makes college football great.

The tradition, which started in 2017, has evolved into a moment for everyone to take part of. The UI Stead Family Children's Hospital staff love being part of the ongoing tradition with Iowa athletics.

Clark being able to come home and experience this on the other side has to be thrilling. The three-time WNBA All-Star for the Indiana Fever was bounced from the playoffs early by the Las Vegas Aces this week.
